intro.data: Now you get two converters for each kind of data, both shaped right (a List in, an Optional out). Only one is trustworthy: it gives the same answer whether you transform the items first and then take the head, or take the head first and then transform. safeHead does. headOrDefault invents a default when the list is empty — and an invented item has nothing real to transform, so the two orders disagree. Pick the converter that always agrees, for every kind of data.
intro.alchemy: Now you get two methods for each reagent, both the right shape (a rack in, a single vial out). Only one is trustworthy: it gives the same result whether you refine the vials first and then take one, or take the first vial and then refine it. 'Take First' does. 'First or Conjure' conjures a blank vial when the rack is bare — and a conjured vial has nothing real to refine, so the two orders disagree. Pick the method that always agrees, for every reagent.
intro.spellcraft: Now you get two workings for each essence, both the right shape (a stack in, a single rune out). Only one is trustworthy: it gives the same result whether you transform the runes first and then take one, or take the top rune and then transform it. 'Take Top' does. 'Top or Conjure' conjures a blank rune when the stack is empty — and a conjured rune has nothing real to transform, so the two orders disagree. Choose the working that always agrees, for every essence.
intro.abstract: Two candidate components α_A are offered at each object, both F(A) → G(A). Only one family is natural: α_B ∘ F(f) = G(f) ∘ α_A for every f. Choose it.

afterSuccess.data: safeHead gave the same result whichever order you worked in. headOrDefault didn't — its invented default breaks on the empty list, since a made-up item has nothing real to transform. Matching shapes weren't enough; the two orders had to agree. That agreement is what makes a rule natural.
afterSuccess.alchemy: 'Take First' gave the same result whichever order you worked in. 'First or Conjure' didn't — its conjured vial breaks on the empty rack, since a conjured vial has nothing real to refine. Matching shapes weren't enough; the two orders had to agree. That agreement is what makes a rule natural.
afterSuccess.spellcraft: 'Take Top' gave the same result whichever order you worked in. 'Top or Conjure' didn't — its conjured rune breaks on the empty stack, since a conjured rune has nothing real to transform. Matching shapes weren't enough; the two orders had to agree. That agreement is what makes a working natural.
afterSuccess.abstract: Only the natural family commutes; the typed-but-broken family fails the square. Correct typing is necessary but not sufficient.

reveal.summary: Naturality: for every f : A → B, α_B ∘ F(f) = G(f) ∘ α_A. A family of correctly-typed components is a natural transformation only when every such square commutes.
reveal.moreFormal: This puzzle checks naturality for real: the engine composes both ways around each square using D's composition table and compares. headOrDefault is well-typed but not natural.
reveal.programmerAnalogy: A polymorphic function is natural (a 'parametric' one); injecting a fixed default breaks parametricity.
